The Invoice That Changed Everything

Six invoices on the desk. Three discrepancies found. The audit begins.

The Full Story

Carolina Mendes has been managing procurement at Althea Industrial for three years. Last month, something small turned into something serious. An invoice from Hua Li Components was received by the accounts team on a Tuesday, but the amount was different from what had been agreed in the Purchase Order. Carolina has already sent two formal emails to Kevin Chen, Hua Li's account manager, asking for an explanation. According to the contract, any price change is supposed to be communicated in writing at least 14 days before the invoice date. That step was never taken.

Kevin has responded to Carolina's second email, saying the difference was caused by a raw material surcharge that had been applied to all international clients since January. Carolina has not accepted this explanation, because Althea's contract was signed with fixed pricing until June. She thinks the surcharge should have been flagged during the quarterly review, not discovered by accident on an invoice. A formal dispute has been opened by the legal team.

The disputed amount is 4,200 USD. Under the contract, any invoice dispute is supposed to be resolved within 30 business days. Carolina has asked her finance director to hold payment on the full invoice until the dispute is closed. Hua Li has not agreed to a payment hold, arguing that the undisputed portion should be paid immediately. A meeting between both legal teams has been scheduled for the following week.

Meanwhile, Carolina has reviewed the last six invoices from Hua Li and found two other small discrepancies that had been overlooked at the time. Those amounts were never disputed, so they have already been paid. Carolina thinks an internal audit should have been conducted sooner, and has asked her team to set up a monthly invoice verification process.

Kevin has also offered to provide a credit note for the surcharge if Althea signs a new pricing agreement valid from January. This offer has not been accepted by Carolina, because signing a new agreement would mean accepting the surcharge retroactively. Under the current contract, any new pricing terms are supposed to be negotiated before they take effect, not imposed after the fact.

The finance director has agreed with Carolina's position and has sent a formal letter to Hua Li stating that Althea will not sign any backdated agreement. The letter also states that Hua Li is supposed to provide a corrected invoice within five business days or the dispute will be escalated to arbitration.

Grammar Guide
Passive Voice
Voz passiva

Use when the action matters more than who did it. Structure: be + past participle.

Claim: "The invoice was received on Tuesday."→Was the invoice received on Tuesday?
SimpleThe invoice was received.
PerfectA dispute has been opened.
ModalIt should have been flagged.
Supposed To
Dever / Era para

Describes an obligation, rule, or expectation. Often means the rule exists — but may not have been followed.

Claim: "The change is supposed to be communicated in writing."→Is the change supposed to be communicated in writing?
Present Perfect
Presente perfeito

Connects a past action to the present moment. Structure: have/has + past participle.

Claim: "Carolina has sent two formal emails."→Has Carolina sent two formal emails?
